#1
L: That brahman — what [is it]? Adhyātma — what? Action — what, O Supreme Person? And what is called adhibhūta, and what is adhidaiva called?
I: What is that brahman? What is the individual self? What is action, Supreme Person? What is called material existence, and what is called the divine order?
N: This opens the chapter as Arjuna's question, continuing directly from the end of chapter 7, whose closing verses (7.29-30) first named these very terms — brahman, adhyātma, karman, adhibhūta, adhidaiva — without defining them; Kṛṣṇa answers each in turn at 8.3-4, in the same order Arjuna asks them here. Puruṣottama, 'highest of persons', is rendered 'Supreme Person' wherever it occurs; the word's own entry gives the two senses it can carry in Arjuna's mouth. Sandhi: तद्ब्रह्म is tat + brahma; किमध्यात्मं, प्रोक्तमधिदैवं and किमुच्यते all show a final -m simply written joined before a following vowel, with no phonetic change (kim+adhyātmam, proktam+adhidaivam, kim+ucyate).
#2
L: Adhiyajña — how, who [is it] here in this body, O slayer of Madhu? And at the time of departure, how are you to be known by those of controlled mind?
I: How, and who, is the lord of sacrifice here in this body, Madhusūdana? And how are you to be known, at the time of death, by those whose minds are controlled?
N: Arjuna's question continues, now asking after adhiyajña, the fourth term named at the end of chapter 7 (7.30) but not yet defined, and adding a fifth question of his own — how Kṛṣṇa is to be recognized at the moment of death (prayāṇa-kāle), which this chapter returns to repeatedly (verses 5-13). Madhusūdana, 'slayer of Madhu', an epithet of Kṛṣṇa recalling his defeat of the demon Madhu. Sandhi: कोऽत्र is kaḥ + atra; देहेऽस्मिन्मधुसूदन packs dehe + asmin (avagraha) + madhusūdana (no further change); ज्ञेयोऽसि is jñeyaḥ + asi.
#3
L: The imperishable, supreme, [is] brahman; own-nature is called adhyātma. That which causes the coming-into-existence of beings' existence, the emission, is called action.
I: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; one's own essential nature is called the individual self. The creative outpouring that causes beings to come into existence is called action.
N: Kṛṣṇa now answers Arjuna's first two questions from verses 1-2, in order: brahman is identified with akṣaram, 'the imperishable' (paramam, 'supreme', qualifying it); adhyātma is defined as svabhāva, 'one's own essential nature'. The third answer, on karman, follows in the second half: action is defined as visarga, the 'emission' or 'creative discharge', bhūta-bhāva-udbhava-karaḥ, 'that which causes the existence of beings to arise' — the cosmic outflow of activity by which beings come into being, not merely ritual or moral action. Karman itself is translated throughout, unlike brahman, dharma, yoga, the guṇas and sāṃkhya, which stay untranslated. Sandhi: स्वभावोऽध्यात्ममुच्यते packs svabhāvaḥ + adhyātmam (avagraha) + ucyate (joined, no change); भूतभावोद्भवकरो packs bhūta + bhāva + udbhava (a+u→o) + karaḥ (-aḥ before v- → -o).
#4
L: Adhibhūta [is] the perishable state; and puruṣa [is] adhidaivata. Adhiyajña, here in the body, [is] I myself, indeed, O best of the embodied.
I: Material existence is the perishable state, and the Person is the divine order. And the lord of sacrifice, here in the body, is I myself, best of embodied beings.
N: Kṛṣṇa completes the answer: adhibhūta, 'material existence', is kṣaraḥ bhāvaḥ, 'the perishable state' — set against akṣara, 'the imperishable', of verse 3; adhidaiva (here spelled adhidaivatam) is identified with puruṣaḥ, 'the Person', traditionally read as the totality of the gods or of the sense-faculties viewed as divine; and adhiyajña, 'the lord of sacrifice', Kṛṣṇa identifies directly with himself, present within the body (dehe) — the fifth and last term named at 7.30, now defined. Deha-bhṛtāṃ vara, 'O best of embodied beings', addresses Arjuna as a representative of all embodied souls. Sandhi: पुरुषश्चाधिदैवतम् packs puruṣaḥ + ca (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-) + adhidaivatam (a+a→ā); अधियज्ञोऽहमेवात्र packs adhiyajñaḥ + aham (avagraha) + eva + atra (a+a→ā).
#5
L: And at the time of the end, remembering me alone, having released the body — who thus departs, he attains my state of being; there is no doubt here.
I: And at the moment of death, remembering me alone as he leaves the body, whoever departs thus attains my own being; of this there is no doubt.
N: This opens the chapter's recurring theme, first raised by Arjuna's question at verse 2: what determines a person's fate at the moment of death is what is remembered then (cf. verses 6, 10, 13). Sandhi: नास्त्यत्र packs na + asti (nā-) + atra (-i+a-→-y a-); स is saḥ with its visarga dropped before the consonant m- (a fixed rule for the pronoun forms saḥ and eṣaḥ, which never take -o before a consonant).
#6
L: Whatever state, remembering, he abandons the body at the end — that very [state] he attains, O son of Kuntī, always having been habituated to that state.
I: Whatever state a man remembers when he finally leaves the body, that very state he attains, Kaunteya, ever having been steeped in it.
N: This generalizes verse 5: the state one attains at death is always whatever bhāva, 'state of being', one is habituated to through life (sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ) — a principle Kṛṣṇa uses in verse 7 to urge constant remembrance of himself specifically. Yaṃ yaṃ ... taṃ tam, doubled relative and correlative pronouns, are the standard distributive construction, 'whatever ... that same' (cf. 7.21's yo yo ... tasya tasya). Sandhi: वापि is vā + api; त्यजत्यन्ते is tyajati + ante; तमेवैति packs tam + eva + eti (a+e→ai).
#7
L: Therefore, at all times remember me and fight. With mind and intellect fixed on me, you shall go to me alone, without doubt.
I: So keep me in mind at all times, and fight. With your mind and intellect fixed on me, you will surely come to me, beyond doubt.
N: This draws the practical conclusion from verses 5-6: since one becomes at death whatever one has dwelt on in life, Arjuna should remember Kṛṣṇa constantly even while fighting. The whole second line is written in the source as a single unbroken string, मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्मामेवैष्यस्यसंशयम्, packing five words: mayi + arpita-manaḥ-buddhiḥ + mām + eva + eṣyasi + asaṃśayam. The vulgate text printed and drafted here ends the verse with असंशयम्, asaṃśayam, an adverbial accusative, 'you shall come to me, without doubt'; the BORI critical edition (GRETIL, Tokunaga-Smith) reads instead असंशयः, asaṃśayaḥ, nominative — 'you shall come to me; there is no doubt' — as a separate clause. This is a real vulgate/BORI variant (listed as such in parts.json); the vulgate reading is the one printed here.
#8
L: By a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not going to another [object] — the supreme divine Person he attains, O son of Pṛthā, continually contemplating [him].
I: With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not straying to any other object, one attains the supreme divine Person, Pārtha, by dwelling on him without ceasing.
N: Abhyāsa-yoga, 'the yoga of [repeated] practice', names the discipline of habituation urged in verses 6-7: a mind trained not to wander (an-anya-gāmin, 'not going elsewhere') and kept in constant contemplation (anucintayan) is what reaches paramaṃ puruṣaṃ divyam, 'the supreme divine Person', the object first named at verse 4 as adhidaiva. Sandhi: नान्यगामिना is na + anya-gāminā; पार्थानुचिन्तयन् is pārtha + anucintayan.
#9
L: The seer, the ancient, the ruler, smaller than the atom — [him] who meditates on, the ordainer of all, of inconceivable form, sun-colored, beyond darkness —
I: Whoever meditates on the ancient seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtlest atom, the sustainer of all, of inconceivable form, radiant as the sun, beyond the reach of darkness —
N: This begins a single sentence completed only at verse 10 (sa taṃ paraṃ puruṣam upaiti, 'he attains that supreme Person'): a relative clause (yaḥ ... anusmaret, 'whoever meditates on') piling up epithets for the object of meditation. Both half-lines are written in the source as long fused strings with a break only after their first word: पुराणमनुशासितारमणोरणीयांसमनुस्मरेद्यः packs purāṇam + anuśāsitāram + aṇoḥ + aṇīyāṃsam + anusmaret + yaḥ, and धातारमचिन्त्यरूपमादित्यवर्णं packs dhātāram + acintya-rūpam + āditya-varṇam. Aṇor aṇīyāṃsam, 'smaller than the atom, subtler than the subtle', is a standard formula for the ungraspable minuteness of the supreme self. Unlike verses 10, 11 and 28, this verse's two long lines are drafted here as an ordinary two-line block, following the source's own line division.
#10
L: At the time of departure, with unwavering mind, endowed with devotion, and by the power of yoga indeed, having fixed the breath correctly between the eyebrows — he attains that supreme divine Person.
I: At the hour of death, with a mind that does not waver, filled with devotion, and by the strength of yoga, fixing the breath rightly between the eyebrows, he reaches that supreme, divine Person.
N: This completes the sentence begun in verse 9, describing the practice by which the object of meditation described there is reached: an unwavering mind (manasā acalena), devotion (bhaktyā), the power of yoga, and the yogic technique of fixing the breath between the eyebrows at death (bhruvor madhye prāṇam āveśya) — the same moment of death addressed since verse 5. This is the chapter's first four-line verse (triṣṭubh meter rather than the ordinary two-line śloka), so its words.txt block has three line-breaks rather than one. Sandhi: मनसाचलेन is manasā + acalena; भ्रुवोर्मध्ये is bhruvoḥ + madhye; प्राणमावेश्य is prāṇam + āveśya; पुरुषमुपैति is puruṣam + upaiti.
#11
L: Which imperishable the knowers of the Veda declare, which the passionless strivers enter, desiring which they practice the discipline of brahman (chastity) — that state to you in summary I shall declare.
I: That imperishable reality the knowers of the Veda speak of, that the passionless ascetics enter, that which seekers practice chastity to attain — I will now tell you that state in brief.
N: A triple-relative construction (yat ... yat ... yat, 'which ... which ... which', each governing a different verb) builds up a description of akṣara, 'the imperishable' — the same term brahman was identified with at verse 3 — before Kṛṣṇa announces he will now explain it 'in brief' (saṃgraheṇa), which he does through the rest of the chapter. Brahmacaryam, literally 'the discipline pertaining to brahman', is the traditional term for celibate religious studentship; brahman itself stays untranslated per convention, so the compound is rendered literally in L. This is the second of the chapter's three four-line (triṣṭubh) verses. Sandhi: यदक्षरं, यद्यतयो and यदिच्छन्तो each show yat losing its -t before the next consonant/vowel (-t+a-→-d a-; -t+y-→-d y-; -t+i-→-d i-); वेदविदो, यद्यतयो and यदिच्छन्तो all show a final -aḥ becoming -o before a voiced consonant.
#12
L: Having restrained all the gates, and confined the mind in the heart, and having fixed one's own breath in the head, established in yogic concentration —
I: Restraining every gate of the body, confining the mind within the heart, fixing the life-breath in the head, and settling into yogic concentration —
N: This begins the sentence completed at verse 13 (yaḥ prayāti ... sa yāti paramāṃ gatim, 'he who thus departs attains the supreme goal'), describing the yogic technique of dying consciously: withdrawing from the sense-gates (sarva-dvārāṇi), confining the mind in the heart, and raising the breath to the crown of the head (mūrdhni) — the same head-crown site implied at verse 10's 'between the eyebrows'. Sandhi: मूर्ध्न्याधायात्मनः packs mūrdhni + ādhāya (i+ā→yā) + ātmanaḥ (a+ā→ā); प्राणमास्थितो is prāṇam + āsthitaḥ.
#13
L: Om — thus the single-syllabled brahman — uttering, remembering me: who thus departs, abandoning the body, he attains the supreme goal.
I: Uttering the single syllable Om, that is brahman, and remembering me, whoever departs, leaving the body behind, reaches the highest goal.
N: Om, the sacred monosyllable used to open Vedic recitation (cf. 7.8's praṇavaḥ sarva-vedeṣu, 'the syllable Om in all the Vedas'), is here called eka-akṣaram, 'the single syllable' — a different sense of akṣara from its use as 'the imperishable' at verses 3, 11 and 21, though the two senses are traditionally felt as one word, the syllable itself being 'imperishable'. This continues the death-meditation instructions of verses 10 and 12: uttering Om while remembering Kṛṣṇa, at the moment of leaving the body, leads to the supreme goal. Sandhi: ओमित्येकाक्षरं packs om + iti (joined) + eka-akṣaram (i+e→ye); व्याहरन्मामनुस्मरन् packs vyāharan + mām + anusmaran (all joined without change); त्यजन्देहं is tyajan + deham.
#14
L: Whose mind is on nothing else, who constantly, unceasingly remembers me — of him, I [am] easy to attain, O son of Pṛthā, of that ever-disciplined yogin.
I: For the yogin whose mind is fixed on nothing else, who remembers me constantly and without fail, I am easy to reach, Pārtha — for one who is always so disciplined.
N: This shifts from the moment of death to the discipline of a lifetime: ananya-cetāḥ, 'whose mind is on nothing else', and nitya-yuktasya yoginaḥ, 'of the ever-disciplined yogin', describe the same constancy of remembrance urged since verse 7, now promised an easy reward (sulabhaḥ, 'easy to attain'). Sandhi: तस्याहं is tasya + aham (a+a→ā).
#15
L: Having reached me, great souls, having attained the supreme perfection, do not obtain rebirth, an abode of suffering, not eternal.
I: Great souls who reach me, having attained the highest perfection, are not born again into this fleeting abode of suffering.
N: Punarjanma, 'rebirth', is defined here as duḥkha-ālayam aśāśvatam, 'an impermanent abode of suffering' — the fate that souls who attain Kṛṣṇa (mām upetya) and the highest perfection (saṃsiddhiṃ paramāṃ gatāḥ) escape, a claim the next verse contrasts with rebirth even in the highest heavens short of Kṛṣṇa himself. Sandhi: नाप्नुवन्ति is na + āpnuvanti (ā-); महात्मानः is mahā + ātmānaḥ (ā+ā→ā); दुःखालयमशाश्वतम् packs duḥkha + ālayam (a+ā→ā) + aśāśvatam (joined, no change).
#16
L: The worlds up to the world of Brahmā [are] subject to return again, O Arjuna; but having reached me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist.
I: All the worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, are worlds one returns from, Arjuna; but for one who reaches me, Kaunteya, there is no rebirth.
N: This confirms verse 15 by contrast: even ā-brahma-bhuvanāt lokāḥ, 'the worlds as far as the world of Brahmā' — the highest heavens attainable by ordinary merit, including Brahmā's own realm — are punar-āvartinaḥ, 'subject to return', still within the cycle of rebirth; only reaching Kṛṣṇa himself (mām upetya) ends it, restating punar-janma na vidyate, 'there is no rebirth', in the same terms as verse 15's escape from duḥkhālayam aśāśvatam. Sandhi: आब्रह्मभुवनाल्लोकाः is ā-brahma-bhuvanāt + lokāḥ (-āt+l-→-āl l-); पुनरावर्तिनोऽर्जुन packs punar + āvartinaḥ (avagraha before arjuna).
#17
L: Which day, having a thousand ages as its limit, [is] Brahmā's — they know; and the night, having a thousand ages as its end — those people [are] the knowers of day and night.
I: The day of Brahmā, they know, lasts a thousand ages, and his night lasts as long — those who understand this understand what day and night truly are.
N: Brahmaṇaḥ, 'of Brahmā' (the creator-god), and brahman, the untranslated absolute of verses 3 and 24, are the same word in different senses — here specifically the personal creator-deity, whose single day (a kalpa) and single night each last sahasra-yuga-paryantam, 'a thousand cosmic ages', a scale against which the death-and-rebirth described in verses 15-16 is measured. Sandhi: the whole first half-line is written as one fused string, सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो, packing sahasra-yuga-paryantam + ahaḥ (as ahar- before the vowel-initial yat) + yat (-t+b-→-d b-) + brahmaṇaḥ (-aḥ before v- → -o); तेऽहोरात्रविदो packs te (avagraha) + ahaḥ (as aho- before r-) + rātra + vidaḥ (-aḥ before j- → -o).
#18
L: From the unmanifest, all manifestations arise, at the coming of day; at the coming of night, they dissolve, into that very [same principle] called 'the unmanifest'.
I: At the break of day, all manifest things spring forth from the unmanifest; at the fall of night, they dissolve back into that same unmanifest state.
N: This turns from the day and night of Brahmā (verse 17) to a smaller-scale cosmic cycle: at each 'day', all vyaktayaḥ, 'manifestations' (created things), emerge from avyakta, 'the unmanifest' (a term returned to at verses 20-21 as a name for the ultimate reality beyond even this cycle); at each 'night' they dissolve back into it. Sandhi: अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः is avyaktāt + vyaktayaḥ (-āt+v-→-ād v-); प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे packs prabhavanti (-i+a-→-y a-) + ahaḥ (as ahar- before the vowel ā-); रात्र्यागमे is rātri + āgame (i+ā→yā); तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके packs tatra + eva (a+e→ai) + avyakta (a+a→ā) + saṃjñake.
#19
L: That very same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves, powerless, O son of Pṛthā, at the coming of night, [and] comes forth again at the coming of day.
I: This same host of beings, coming into existence over and over, helplessly dissolves at nightfall and springs forth again at daybreak, Pārtha.
N: This restates verse 18 with the emphasis on the beings' own helplessness: avaśaḥ, 'without control, powerless', describes the bhūta-grāmaḥ, 'multitude of beings', caught in this cycle of arising and dissolving, in contrast to the unconditioned freedom Kṛṣṇa promised at verses 15-16 to those who reach him. Sandhi: एवायं is eva + ayam; रात्र्यागमेऽवशः packs rātri + āgame (i+ā→yā) + avaśaḥ (avagraha); प्रभवत्यहरागमे as in verse 18.
#20
L: But beyond that there is another state, unmanifest, beyond the unmanifest, eternal — which, among all beings perishing, does not perish.
I: But beyond that cycle there is another reality, unmanifest, beyond even the unmanifest, everlasting — which does not perish when all beings perish.
N: Tasmāt, 'than that', refers back to the whole cycle of manifestation and dissolution of verses 18-19; this bhāvaḥ anyaḥ avyaktaḥ, 'another state, [also called] unmanifest', is explicitly distinguished from that avyaktāt, 'unmanifest' (the same word used again, now for a second, higher reality) — a distinction the next verse names directly as akṣara, 'the imperishable'. Sandhi: परस्तस्मात्तु is paraḥ + tasmāt (-aḥ+t-→-as t-) + tu; भावोऽन्योऽव्यक्तोऽव्यक्तात्सनातनः packs bhāvaḥ + anyaḥ + avyaktaḥ (each -aḥ+a-→-o with avagraha) + avyaktāt + sanātanaḥ (no further change, t+s stays).
#21
L: The unmanifest, called 'the imperishable' — that they call the supreme goal. Having attained which, they do not turn back — that [is] my supreme abode.
I: That unmanifest reality, called 'the imperishable', is what they call the highest goal; having reached it, none return — that is my highest abode.
N: This names the 'other, unmanifest state' of verse 20 directly: it is avyaktaḥ akṣaraḥ, 'the unmanifest, [also called] the imperishable' — the same akṣara that verse 3 identified with brahman — and Kṛṣṇa here calls it tad dhāma paramaṃ mama, 'my own supreme abode'. Sandhi: अव्यक्तोऽक्षर is avyaktaḥ + akṣaraḥ (-aḥ+a-→-o with avagraha); the visarga of akṣaraḥ itself, before the vowel इति that begins the next word, simply drops without further vowel fusion, which is why the source keeps a space here rather than merging the two words further; इत्युक्तस्तमाहुः packs iti + uktaḥ (i+u→yu) + tam (-aḥ+t-→-as t-) + āhuḥ (joined); तद्धाम is tat + dhāma (-t+dh-→-d dh-).
#22
L: That Person is supreme, O son of Pṛthā, attainable by undivided devotion — within whom beings dwell, by whom this all is pervaded.
I: That supreme Person, Pārtha, can be reached only through undivided devotion — the one within whom all beings dwell, and by whom this whole universe is pervaded.
N: This returns to puruṣaḥ, 'the Person', last named at verse 8 as the goal of unwavering practice, now specified as reachable bhaktyā tu ananyayā, 'only by undivided devotion' — echoing 7.17's eka-bhaktiḥ, 'single-minded devotion' — and described in terms recalling 7.7's image of the world strung on Kṛṣṇa like jewels on a thread (yasya antaḥsthāni bhūtāni yena sarvam idaṃ tatam). Sandhi: लभ्यस्त्वनन्यया packs labhyaḥ (-aḥ+t-→-as t-) + tu (u+a→va, yaṇ) + ananyayā; यस्यान्तःस्थानि is yasya + antaḥsthāni (a+a→ā); सर्वमिदं is sarvam + idam.
#23
L: At which time, but, to non-return and to return as well, yogins, having departed, go — that time I shall declare, O bull among the Bharatas.
I: The time at which yogins depart to reach non-return, and the time at which they depart and return again — that time I will now explain to you, bull among the Bharatas.
N: This announces the topic of verses 24-26: the two 'times' or 'paths' of departure from the body, one leading to anāvṛtti, 'non-return' (freedom from rebirth), the other to āvṛtti, 'return' (rebirth) — a teaching Kṛṣṇa says he will now declare (vakṣyāmi), picking up the promise of verse 11 to explain akṣara saṃgraheṇa, 'in brief'. Sandhi: त्वनावृत्तिमावृत्तिं packs tu (u+a→va) + anāvṛttim + āvṛttim (joined); प्रयाता is prayātāḥ with its visarga dropped before यान्ति (voiced y-).
#24
L: Fire, light, day, the bright [fortnight], the six months of the northern course — there departing, they go to brahman, the people who are knowers of brahman.
I: Fire, light, day, the bright half of the month, the six months of the sun's northern course — departing at such a time, those who know brahman go to brahman.
N: This gives the path of non-return promised in verse 23: a list of five ascending markers — fire, light, day, the bright (waxing) fortnight, and the six months of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa, when the sun appears to move northward) — traditionally read as the successive stages of the 'path of the gods', by which brahma-vidaḥ, 'knowers of brahman', reach brahman itself without return. Sandhi: अग्निर्ज्योतिरहः packs agniḥ (-iḥ+j-→-ir j-) + jyotiḥ (-iḥ+a-→-ir); षण्मासा is ṣaṭ + māsāḥ (-ṭ+m-→-ṇ m-) with its own visarga then dropped before उत्तरायणम्; उत्तरायणम् is uttara + ayanam (a+a→ā); प्रयाता is prayātāḥ, visarga dropped before गच्छन्ति; ब्रह्मविदो is brahma-vidaḥ, -aḥ before j- → -o.
#25
L: Smoke, night, likewise, the dark [fortnight], the six months of the southern course — there, having reached the lunar light, the yogin returns.
I: Smoke, night, the dark half of the month, the six months of the sun's southern course — by that path the yogin reaches the light of the moon, and returns.
N: This gives the counterpart path of return: smoke, night, the dark (waning) fortnight, and the six months of the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) — traditionally the 'path of the ancestors' — by which a yogin reaches only cāndramasaṃ jyotiḥ, 'the light of the moon' (a lesser, temporary heaven), and then nivartate, 'returns' to rebirth, unlike the brahma-vidaḥ of verse 24. Sandhi: धूमो is dhūmaḥ, -aḥ before r- → -o; रात्रिस्तथा is rātriḥ + tathā (-iḥ+t-→-is t-); षण्मासा as in verse 24; दक्षिणायनम् is dakṣiṇa + ayanam (a+a→ā); ज्योतिर्योगी is jyotiḥ + yogī (-iḥ+y-→-ir y-).
#26
L: Bright and dark — these two [are] the world's eternal paths, so held; by one, [the soul] goes to non-return, by the other it returns again.
I: The bright path and the dark — these two are held to be the world's everlasting courses; by one the soul goes to no return, by the other it comes back again.
N: This sums up verses 24-25 by naming the two courses śukla and kṛṣṇa, 'bright' and 'dark', as jagataḥ śāśvate gatī mate, 'the world's two eternal paths', with ekayā ... anyayā, 'by one ... by the other', picking up each path's outcome directly from the preceding two verses. Sandhi: ह्येते is hi + ete (i+e→ye); यात्यनावृत्तिमन्ययावर्तते packs yāti (-i+a-→-y a-) + anāvṛttim + anyayā + āvartate (a+ā→ā).
#27
L: Not these two paths, knowing, is the yogin confused, any at all, O son of Pṛthā; therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.
I: No yogin who knows these two paths is ever confused, Pārtha; so at all times remain disciplined in yoga, Arjuna.
N: This closes the teaching on the two paths (sṛtī, another word for 'path', echoing gatī of verse 26): knowing them removes all confusion for a yogin, and Kṛṣṇa draws the same practical conclusion as verse 7 — constant discipline in yoga at every moment. Sandhi: नैते is na + ete; तस्मात्सर्वेषु as in verse 7; योगयुक्तो is yoga-yuktaḥ, -aḥ before bh- → -o; भवार्जुन is bhava + arjuna (a+a→ā).
#28
L: Whatever meritorious fruit is declared [to belong] to [rites of] the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts — the yogin, having known all this, goes beyond [it] and attains the supreme, primal station.
I: Whatever reward is promised for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and acts of giving, the yogin, knowing all this, transcends it and reaches the supreme, primal abode.
N: The chapter's closing, third four-line verse sums up its whole argument: the merits promised for the Vedic disciplines named here — study of the Vedas, sacrifice, austerity, giving — are all finite (cf. 7.23's antavat phalam), and the yogin who has understood everything taught since verse 5 goes beyond them all (atyeti) to param sthānam ādyam, 'the supreme, primal station' — Kṛṣṇa's own abode named at verse 21. Sandhi: चैव is ca + eva; तत्सर्वमिदं packs tat + sarvam + idam (all joined without change); स्थानमुपैति is sthānam + upaiti; चाद्यम् is ca + ādyam (a+ā→ā).
